quote:
month_name has to turn a 1-based month index into the full English month name, and indices below 1 or above 12 must be folded back into range with modular arithmetic, so 13 means January and 0 means December.

The body builds a list holding the twelve names in calendar order and then does the conversion in two lines:

        idx = (month_index - 1) % 12
        return names[idx]

Subtracting one moves the index onto a zero-based scale that lines up with list positions, and the modulo then folds any integer into the range 0 through 11. Python's % operator gives a non-negative result whenever the divisor is positive, which is the property that makes the wrap work for negative arguments as well as for large ones. The three visible calls use 1, 6 and 12, all already inside the normal range, so on their own they say nothing about wrapping.

Because wrapping is the part the examples leave unexercised, I worked through a few out-of-range values. For 0 the adjusted value is -1, and -1 % 12 is 11, which selects December, exactly the case the spec mentions. For 13 the adjusted value 12 reduces to 0 and yields January. For -1 the position is 10, giving November, and for 25 the position is 0 again, giving January. Each of these agrees with counting months forward or backward around the calendar. There is no branch keyed to particular arguments; every integer goes through the same subtraction, remainder and list lookup, so the month names come out right across the whole integer range rather than only for the three sample months.
